anf_compare.notes: Translated from the PG 74 Greek; no published English version was used for wording.

bible_refs.note: Ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω, introduced as said 'to Moses'; matches LXX Exodus 33:19 (same numbering).
Paul quotes the same Exodus text in Romans 9:15 (λέγει τῷ Μωϋσεῖ); both cited because Cyril is expounding the Romans lemma.
Direct quotation: ἄρα οὖν οὐ τοῦ θέλοντος οὐδὲ τοῦ τρέχοντος ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐλεῶντος θεοῦ (Cyril: ἐλεοῦντος).
Direct quotation of Paul's form: εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε ὅπως ἐνδείξωμαι ἐν σοὶ τὴν δύναμίν μου.
Source of Romans 9:17; LXX reads ἕνεκεν τούτου διετηρήθης ἵνα ἐνδείξωμαι ἐν σοὶ τὴν ἰσχύν μου. Cyril follows Paul's wording; same numbering in LXX and Hebrew.
Direct quotation: ἄρα οὖν ὃν θέλει ἐλεεῖ, ὃν δὲ θέλει σκληρύνει.
Direct quotation: ἐρεῖς μοι οὖν· τί ἔτι μέμφεται; τῷ γὰρ βουλήματι αὐτοῦ τίς ἀνθέστηκεν;

Quoted in full (ὦ ἄνθρωπε, μενοῦνγε σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενος τῷ θεῷ; μὴ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα τῷ πλάσαντι· τί με ἐποίησας οὕτως;) and its second half repeated at the end of the row; Paul draws on Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9, which Cyril does not cite here.

pass_a_gloss: …knowledge (γνῶσιν) those whom he might perhaps choose, but rather also those to whom it might fittingly befit (πρέποι) to be shown mercy (ἐλεεῖσθαι), he pities (οἰκτείρει) again as God, for he said somewhere to Moses 'I will have mercy (ἐλεήσω) on whom I have mercy and I will pity whom I pity,' how will the thing not be outside all slander (διαβολῆς)? And the apostle, I think, having clearly looked ahead (προαναθρήσας) that perhaps some will think by the divine nods (νεύμασι) some to be good, others disobedient (ἀπειθεῖς), necessarily himself counter-puts (ἀνθυποφέρει) the things from their ignorance (ἀμαθίας) and says 'So then not of the one willing (θέλοντος) nor of the one running (τρέχοντος) but of the God having mercy'; for if indeed Esau has been hated even before doing anything of the base things, and Jacob honoured even before his passage into being (εἰς τὸ εἶναι παρόδου), and again he has mercy on whom he has mercy, how is it not then worthy to think out that the one running or willing profits (ὀνίνησιν) nothing, that is the one eager to do something of the good things, but all things about us hang (ἀπήρτηται) from the nods from God? Then to these he heaps on (ἐπισωρεύει) also the things able further to make firm (προσεμπεδοῦν) the opinion (δόξαν) on this and says 'For the scripture says to Pharaoh that for this very thing I raised you up (ἐξήγειρα) so that I might show in you my power (δύναμιν)'; and he adds to these as it were the conclusion (συμπέρασμα) of the whole problem (προβλήματος) and says 'So then whom he wills he has mercy on, whom he wills he hardens (σκληρύνει); you will say to me then, Why does he still blame (μέμφεται)? For who has stood against (ἀνθέστηκε) his purpose (βουλήματι)?' What then was the manner of his defence (ἀπολογίας)? Very unclear (ἀσυμφανής), and perhaps seeming also to aid (ἐπαμύνειν) the problems from them; but sufficing (ἀποχρῶν) for full assurance, that nothing of the things outside the account of the fitting (πρέποντος) would come about from God; for he distributes (διανέμει) to each the fitting for him, and pities and has mercy on those for whom it might suit to need to be shown mercy, and brings under penalties (δίκαις) the sinner (ἀλιτήριον), wrath (ὀργῆς) not following immediately and at the foot of the charges (αἰτιαμάτων), but rather long forbearance (ἀνεξικακίας) rushing in before, so that some somewhere think God to have then disregarded (ἀφειδῆσαι) those on the earth. So Paul leads out against (ἀντεξάγει), and stands up against those saying those things, letting loose (ἐπαφείς) the force of the word upon the persons (προσώπῳ) of those adduced (παρενηνεγμένων), Esau I say and indeed also Pharaoh. He said then as toward each of those named 'O man, nay rather (μενοῦνγε) who are you answering back (ἀνταποκρινόμενος) to God? Will the moulded thing (πλάσμα) say to the one who moulded (πλάσαντι) Why did you make me thus?' For he shows as from a clear (ἐναργοῦς) example that it is all-hard to rebuke (ἐπιτιμᾶν) divine judgments (κρίμασιν); for if indeed someone should choose to think the fitting things, he will refer (ἀναθήσει) to God who knows all things the judging of each in whatever way he himself knows, and will doubt (ἐνδοιάσει) in nothing that it is holy (ὅσιον) whatever he chooses to do, moulding (διαπλάττων) under authority (ἐπ' ἐξουσίας) the things concerning each perhaps. So he greatly blames those who send into the divine nods at all the testing (βασανίζοντα) mind whether it holds well or not so; for it was needed, he says, that they rather imitate (ἀπομιμεῖσθαι) the thing moulded through a potter's (κεραμέως) hand, and endure with silence (σιγῆς) the things from God; for the moulded thing will not say to the one who moulded, Why did you make me thus? But perhaps also toward this some say that: 'If…'
pass_b_english: …knowledge, he, as God, again has pity on those he may choose, or rather on those to whom it is fitting that mercy be shown, for he said somewhere to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15), then how will the matter not be beyond all reproach?
The apostle, I think, clearly foresaw that some would perhaps suppose that it is by God’s nod that some are good and others disobedient.

So of necessity he himself puts forward the objection that springs from their ignorance, and says, “So then it depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16).

For if Esau was hated even before he had done anything wicked, and Jacob was honoured even before he came into being, and if again God has mercy on whom he has mercy, is it not then right to conclude that the one who runs or wills, that is, the one eager to do something good, gains nothing, and that everything about us hangs on the nods of God?

Then he heaps on top of these the words that could fix that opinion still more firmly, and says, “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you’” (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16).
To these he adds what is, as it were, the conclusion of the whole problem, and says, “So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18).
“You will say to me then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?’” (Romans 9:19).
What, then, was his way of answering?
It is very obscure, and perhaps even seems to support the objections they raise; yet it is enough to assure us that nothing could come from God that lies outside what is fitting.
For he gives to each what befits him: he pities and has mercy on those for whom mercy is fitting, and he subjects the wicked to punishment.
Yet his wrath does not follow the offences at once and on their heels; rather, a long patience goes before it, so that some even suppose that God has stopped caring about those on earth.
So Paul brings out his reply and stands up to those who say such things, directing the force of his words at the persons who had been brought forward, I mean Esau and also Pharaoh.

He spoke, then, as though to each of those he had named: “But who indeed are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is moulded say to the one who moulded it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” (Romans 9:20).
For he shows, as from a plain example, that it is a very grave thing to find fault with God’s judgments.

For if anyone chooses to think as he ought, he will leave to God, who knows all things, the judging of each matter in whatever way God himself knows, and he will not doubt in the least that whatever God chooses to do is holy, as he shapes with full authority whatever concerns each one.
So he sharply blames those who bring a probing mind to bear at all on God’s decrees, as to whether they are right or not.

For they ought, he says, rather to imitate what is moulded by the potter’s hand, and to bear in silence what comes from God, for “what is moulded will not say to the one who moulded it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” (Romans 9:20).
But perhaps some say this in reply as well: “If…”

γνῶσιν οὓς ἂν ἕλοιτο τυχὸν, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ οἷς ἂν εἰκότως τὸ ἐλεεῖσθαι πρέποι,
οἰκτείρει πάλιν 228 ὡς Θεὸς, ἔφη γάρ που πρὸς Μωυσέα Ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ καὶ
οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω, πῶς οὐχ ἁπάσης ἔσται διαβολῆς ἐκτὸς τὸ χρῆμα;
προαναθρήσας δὲ οἶμαι σαφῶς ὁ ἀπόστολος ὡς τάχα που οἰήσονταί τινες νεύμασι τοῖς
θείοις τοὺς μὲν εἶναι ἀγαθοὺς, τοὺς δὲ ἀπειθεῖς, ἀναγκαίως αὐτὸς ἀνθυποφέρει τὰ ἐκ
τῆς ἐκείνων ἀμαθίας καί φησιν Ἄρα οὖν οὐ τοῦ θέλοντος οὐδὲ τοῦ τρέχοντος ἀλλὰ τοῦ
ἐλεοῦντος Θεοῦ· εἰ γὰρ δὴ μεμίσηται μὲν ὁ Ἡσαῦ καὶ πρίν τι δράσαι τῶν φαύλων,
τετίμηται δὲ καὶ πρὸ τῆς εἰς τὸ εἶναι παρόδου ὁ Ἰακὼβ, ἐλεεῖ δὲ πάλιν οὓς ἐλεεῖ, πῶς
οὐκ ἐκεῖνο λοιπὸν περινοεῖν ἄξιον, ὡς οὐδὲν ὀνίνησιν ὁ τρέχων ἢ θέλων, τουτέστιν ὁ
δράσαι τι τῶν ἀγαθῶν προθυμούμενος, ἀπήρτηται δὲ πάντα τὰ καθ' ἡμᾶς τῶν παρὰ
Θεοῦ νευμάτων;
Εἶτα τούτοις ἐπισωρεύει καὶ τὰ προσεμπεδοῦν δυνάμενα τὴν ἐπὶ τῷδε δόξαν καί
φησι Λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφὴ τῷ φαραὼ ὅτι εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε ὅπως ἐνδείξωμαι ἐν
σοὶ τὴν δύναμίν μου· προσεπάγει δὲ τούτοις τὸ οἱονεὶ συμπέρασμα τοῦ παντὸς
προβλήματος καί φησιν Ἄρα οὖν ὃν θέλει ἐλεεῖ, ὃν δὲ θέλει σκληρύνει· ἐρεῖς οὖν μοι Τί
ἔτι μέμφεται; τῷ γὰρ βουλήματι αὐτοῦ τίς ἀνθέστηκε; τίς οὖν ἄρα γέγονεν αὐτῷ τῆς
ἀπολογίας ὁ τρόπος; ἀσυμφανὴς μὲν λίαν, καὶ τοῖς παρ' ἐκείνων προβλήμασι τάχα που
καὶ ἐπαμύνειν δοκῶν· πλὴν ἀποχρῶν εἰς πληροφορίαν, ὡς οὐκ ἂν γένοιτό τι τῶν ἔξω
λόγου τοῦ πρέποντος παρὰ Θεοῦ· διανέμει γὰρ ἑκάστῳ τὸ πρέπον αὐτῷ, κατοικτείρει τε
καὶ ἐλεεῖ τοὺς οἷς ἂν ἁρμόσαι τὸ ἐλεεῖσθαι δεῖν, ὑποφέρει δὲ δίκαις τὸν ἀλιτήριον, οὐκ
εὐθὺς καὶ κατὰ πόδα τῶν αἰτιαμάτων ἀκολουθούσης ὀργῆς, προεισβαλούσης δὲ μᾶλλον

μακρᾶς ἀνεξικακίας, ὡς οἴεσθαί που τινὰς καὶ ἀφειδῆσαι λοιπὸν τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς τὸν

λίαν τοὺς τοῖς θείοις νεύμασιν ἐνιέντας ὅλως τὸν βασανίζοντα νοῦν πότερον καλῶς ἢ

πλαττόμενον, καὶ μετὰ σιγῆς ὑπομένειν τὰ παρὰ Θεοῦ· οὐ γὰρ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα τῷ
πλάσαντι Τί με ἐποίησας οὕτως; Ἀλλ' ἴσως καὶ πρός γε τοῦτό τινες ἐκεῖνό φασιν Εἰ

review_notes: Staged row fixed in tr7.json. Opening dropped ὡς Θεός ('as God') by turning it into a bare subject and added 'his' before γνῶσιν; now '…knowledge, he, as God, again has pity', which joins cleanly to 'But if, in keeping with…' at the end of u08-rem-early. ἴσως … φασιν is present ('some say'), not future ('will reply'). Translator note updated to match.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf), PG columns 227–229.

The row opens mid-sentence: u08-rem-early ends εἰ δὲ δὴ κατὰ, and this row begins γνῶσιν. The English resumes '…knowledge' (completing 'in keeping with' at the end of u08-rem-early) and keeps ὡς Θεός as 'he, as God'; 'then' marks the apodosis πῶς οὐχ … ἔσται.
The row ends at Εἰ, the first word of an objection that continues in u08-rem-close; the English keeps the cut ('If…').
Inline PG column numbers 228 and 229 and page number 23 are print markers and are left out of the English.

The question 'is it not then right to conclude … hangs on the nods of God?' states the inference of those who misread Paul; Cyril's own answer follows from 'What, then, was his way of answering?' The voices are kept distinct.
νεύματα: 'nods', i.e. bare decrees of God's will; kept as 'nod/nods' to preserve Cyril's image.
ἀφειδῆσαι τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς: LSJ ἀφειδέω with genitive 'to disregard, neglect'; rendered 'has stopped caring about those on earth'.

τοῦ λόγου τὴν δύναμιν ἐπαφεὶς τῷ προσώπῳ τῶν παρενηνεγμένων: 'directing the force of his words at the persons who had been brought forward'; Cyril reads Romans 9:20 as addressed to the figures of Esau and Pharaoh.
παγχάλεπον: 'very hard, very grievous'; rendered 'a very grave thing'.
